sentences.text: Tralkasaurus is a genus of abelisaurid dinosaur found in the Huincul Formation of Río Negro Province, Argentina.
This medium-sized predator displays a mix of characteristics from early-diverging forms and the specialized Brachyrostra clade, leaving its exact evolutionary position uncertain.
Scientists describe the animal as a medium-sized member of the abelisaurid family.
The complete creature measured six meters in length.
This upper jaw bone measures twenty-two centimeters in length.
The pubis measures thirty-five centimeters in length.
The maxilla possessed eleven alveoli, four of which contained preserved teeth.
Striations on both edges of the teeth were of the same size.
The front margin of the antorbital fenestra slopes forward and upward, a unique trait among abelisaurids.
Processes on the tail vertebrae projected forward and backward to overlap, a feature typical of the Brachyrostra clade.
The name Tralkasaurus cuyi translates to "thunder lizard of El Cuy," referencing the Mapudungun word for thunder and the discovery village.
Its maxilla is smaller than that of the similarly sized dinosaur Skorpiovenator.
The fossil site was discovered in 1999 by Sebastián Apesteguía near the village of El Cuy in Argentina.
The specific location is the Rancho Violante site near El Cuy in Río Negro province.
The holotype specimen MPCA-Pv 815 consists of an incomplete skeleton including a maxilla, various vertebrae, ribs, and a poorly preserved pubis.
Tralkasaurus was formally described in 2020 by Mauricio Cerroni and colleagues.
Tralkasaurus coexisted with titanosaurian sauropods and an ornithopod in the Huincul Formation ecosystem.
Numerous theropods are known from Rancho Violante, including Gualicho, Aoniraptor, Taurovenator, an unenlagine, and an unnamed carcarodontosaurid.
Other dinosaurs found in the area include a titanosaurian sauropod and an ornithopod.
The animal shares key abelisaurid traits including a deep maxilla, fused interdental plates, specific vertebral connections, inclined tail processes, and a thin pubic shaft.
Phylogenetic analysis places Tralkasaurus among basal abelisaurids but fails to resolve its exact relationship to other species due to conflicting traits.
Tralkasaurus lived in the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, as indicated by the volcanic ash-bearing sandstones of the Huincul Formation.
The habitat was located in what is now South America, specifically in the Huincul Formation of Argentina.
The fossils belong to the Cenomanian-Turonian age of the Huincul Formation.
Tralkasaurus lived during the Albian stage, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago.

Tralkasaurus exhibits a conflicting combination of features, with caudal transverse process projections typical of Brachyrostra but extensive antorbital fossae that are plesiomorphic like basal abelsauroids.
Phylogenetic analysis placed Tralkasaurus as a basal abelisaurid but could not resolve its affinities beyond a polytomy.
